title: Quasi-finite pointwise pinnings and finite detection of residue compatibility
statement:
Let $\ell$ be a prime, $n\geq1$, $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$, and let $X$ be a Noetherian excellent scheme with $\ell$ invertible [def-exc-excellent-ring]. Fix a dimension function $\delta_X$ in the geometric-specialization sense of [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex]. A putative complex is $K\in D^+(X_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)$ with pointwise isomorphisms $p_x:R\Gamma_xK\cong\Lambda(\delta_X(x))[2\delta_X(x)]$, without assuming compatibility with residues; it is potential if that compatibility holds. Let $f:Y\to X$ be a separated [def-weil-proper-morphism] quasi-finite morphism between Noetherian excellent schemes, where quasi-finite means finite type with finite fibres [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Assume a compactification for defining $Rf_!$, and let $f^!$ be its bounded-below exceptional right adjoint [def-amb-etale-compact-support]. Then $\delta_Y=\delta_X\circ f$ is a dimension function and $f^!K$ has induced putative pinnings: for $y\in Y$, $x=f(y)$ and the finite residue-field morphism $\pi:y\to x$ [def-weil-residue-field], use
$$R\Gamma_y(f^!K)\cong\pi^!R\Gamma_xK\xrightarrow{\pi^!p_x}\pi^!\Lambda(\delta_X(x))[2\delta_X(x)]\xrightarrow{\operatorname{Cl}_{\pi}^{-1}}\Lambda(\delta_Y(y))[2\delta_Y(y)].$$
Here $\operatorname{Cl}_{\pi}$ is the finite-field Gysin isomorphism of [lem-per-absolute-gysin-purity] (virtual dimension zero), with the indicated twists. For composable maps these pinnings agree under $g^!f^!\cong(fg)^!$. If $f$ is finite [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism] and surjective [def-weil-surjective-morphism], the induced putative complex $f^!K$ is potential if and only if $K$ is potential.

Use geometric points [def-weil-geometric-point], strict localizations [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit], and normalization in the function field [def-sc-normalization]. Etale restriction to Noetherian etale schemes, localization and strict localization transport putative pinnings and their residue-compatibility squares; these localized schemes are again Noetherian excellent. In a strict localization at $\bar x$, let $i:C\hookrightarrow X_{(\bar x)}$ be the closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] of the reduced closure of a point defining an immediate geometric specialization $\bar y\rightsquigarrow\bar x$. The residue square for $K$ at this specialization is exactly the square for $i^!K$ on $C$ with its induced pinnings. Thus that single compatibility can be tested after the finite surjective normalization of $C$, with the induced exceptional pinnings, without assuming in advance that $K$ or $i^!K$ is potential.

source.place: Expose XVII, Proposition 2.2.1 and the localization observation after it; Proposition 2.4.3.1, Remark 2.4.3.2 and Proposition 2.4.3.3; the reduction to i!K in the proof of Proposition 2.4.4.1, printed pp.264–268.

proof.text: For $y\mapsto x$, the fibre over $x$ is locally of finite type by [lem-weil-pbc-lft-base-change] and is finite discrete by [pqf-lem-locqf-fibre-discrete]. On an affine fibre neighbourhood the singleton of $y$ is open, so [lem-weil-pbc-isolated-prime-finite-type-algebra-residue-finite] makes $\kappa(y)/\kappa(x)$ finite. Its transcendence degree is zero. Excellence includes universal catenarity [def-exc-excellent-ring]; applying [lem-per-finite-type-dimension-function] therefore gives precisely $\delta_Y(y)=\delta_X(f(y))$. This proves the dimension-function assertion, including empty fibres.

source.place: XVII, Proposition 2.4.3.1; dimension-function convention preceding Definition 2.1.1

proof.text: Apply the residue-field comparison of [lem-per-prime-power-supported-calculus] to obtain $C_y(f^!K)\cong\pi^!C_xK$ for this arbitrary putative $K$. Apply $\pi^!$ to $p_x$. For the remaining shifted twisted unit use $\operatorname{Cl}_\pi\otimes1$ followed by $T_\pi(\Lambda,\Lambda(\delta_X(x))[2\delta_X(x)])$ of [lem-per-field-exceptional-tensor]. The Gysin isomorphism [lem-per-absolute-gysin-purity] and the tensor isomorphism make this an isomorphism. Its inverse is the indicated twisted $\operatorname{Cl}_\pi^{-1}$ in the statement. Roots-of-unity pullback identifies the twist on $y$ by [lem-asd-etale-finite-twist-pullback]. Thus the displayed composite gives all the required pointwise pinnings, with no residue condition assumed.

source.place: XVII, Proposition 2.4.3.1, displayed costalk comparison and Gysin construction

proof.text: For $Z\xrightarrow gY\xrightarrow fX$, write $z\mapsto y\mapsto x$ and $b:z\to y$, $a:y\to x$ for the finite field maps. Supported transitivity [lem-per-prime-power-supported-calculus] identifies the two costalk comparisons with $(ab)^!C_xK=b^!a^!C_xK$. The Gysin composition identity of [lem-per-absolute-gysin-purity] is $\operatorname{Cl}_{ab}=b^!(\operatorname{Cl}_a)\circ\operatorname{Cl}_b$; after twists use the counit tensor composition identity in [lem-per-field-exceptional-tensor]. Substituting their inverses into Step 2 gives exactly the direct pinning for $fg$. In particular no degree factor is discarded for an inseparable residue extension.

The localization hypotheses remain valid. Local rings and their localizations are Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-noetherian], and strict henselizations are Noetherian by [lem-sc-strict-henselization-noetherian], using the affine identification [lem-exc-affine-strict-local-ring-comparison]. Localizations and finite-type etale algebras are excellent by [lem-exc-finite-type-localization-excellent]. A strict-localization ring is ind-etale over the affine chart by [lem-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-affine-chart-ind-etale], hence weakly etale by [lem-weil-pbc-ind-etale-stability]; it is excellent by [lem-exc-weakly-etale-excellent]. For an etale restriction take a Noetherian etale scheme, as in Proposition 2.2.1; arbitrary infinite disjoint etale unions need not be Noetherian.

source.place: XVII, Proposition 2.2.1 and the observation immediately following it

proof.text: Etale restrictions, localizations and strict localizations are locally ind-etale: for localizations use the principal-localization colimit [lem-weil-pbc-localization-colimit-principal-localizations], with the open immersions etale by [lem-weil-pbc-open-immersion-etale]; for strict localizations use [lem-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-affine-chart-ind-etale]. By [lem-trf-ind-etale-strict-local-invariance] their strict local schemes at corresponding geometric points are canonically identical. The supported-cohomology comparisons of [lem-per-prime-power-costalk-reduction] therefore identify geometric costalks and the reduced closure and its normalization used to define the transition. On residue-field sites use [lem-per-ind-etale-closed-support-base-change], after passing to affine charts and localizing at the point, to transport the original pinnings. The roots-of-unity comparisons [lem-asd-etale-finite-twist-pullback] identify every twist. Consequently the construction $d^{-1}\operatorname{sp}_{\widetilde C}(\nu^*i^!K)$ in [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex] is the identical map on the two strict local schemes. This proves transport of the actual residue squares, before imposing their commutativity.

source.place: XVII, Proposition 2.2.1 and its localization observation

proof.text: Now let $f$ be finite. Any immediate geometric specialization $\bar v\rightsquigarrow\bar u$ descends to one in $X$: the functorial maps [lem-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-functoriality] give $Y_{(\bar v)}\to Y_{(\bar u)}\to X_{(\bar x)}$, $\bar x=f\bar u$; the image of the closed point of $Y_{(\bar v)}$ is a geometric point of $X_{(\bar x)}$ over $y=f(v)$, and the strict localization of $X_{(\bar x)}$ there is $X_{(\bar y)}$ by [lem-trf-ind-etale-strict-local-invariance], which gives $X_{(\bar y)}\to X_{(\bar x)}$ compatible with the maps from $Y$. It is immediate: by Step 1 its endpoints have $\delta_X$-difference one. By [lem-per-immediate-specialization-criterion] and universal catenarity [def-exc-excellent-ring], a saturated chain between these endpoints has length equal to that difference (add the dimension-function equations at its successive immediate steps); thus its length is one. Conversely, given an immediate $\bar y\rightsquigarrow\bar x$ in $X$, and a geometric lift of $\bar y$, base change to $X_{(\bar x)}$. The finite decomposition [lem-trf-finite-base-strict-localization] puts that lift in a unique strictly local factor $Y_{(\bar u)}$. Its structural map, with the same strict-local identification, gives $\bar v\rightsquigarrow\bar u$ above the chosen specialization. The endpoint dimension difference is again one, so the same chain argument makes this lift immediate. If $f$ is surjective, a geometric lift of $\bar y$ exists by [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-base-change] (its nonempty finite geometric fibre has a geometric point).

source.place: XVII, Propositions 2.3.2–2.3.3 and reduction in Proposition 2.4.3.3

proof.text:
For a pair of immediate specializations as in Step 6, let $B_v,B_u$ be the Gysin-normalized geometric costalk isomorphisms of [lem-per-finite-residue-gysin-naturality]. By naturality of the field tensor map, Step 2's pinnings are $p'_v=p_yB_v^{-1}$ and $p'_u=p_xB_u^{-1}$. That lemma gives, on cohomology, $\operatorname{sp}_Y B_v=B_u(1)[2]\operatorname{sp}_X$. In the present putative situation this is an equality in $D^+(\Lambda)$: both source and target, including the twist and shift, are rank-one free modules concentrated in degree $-2\delta_X(y)$. Maps between these shifted free modules are scalars, determined by that single cohomology group. Hence
$$p'_u(1)[2]\operatorname{sp}_Y=p_x(1)[2]B_u^{-1}(1)[2]\operatorname{sp}_Y=p_x(1)[2]\operatorname{sp}_X B_v^{-1}.$$
Cancel $B_v^{-1}$ to see that $p'_v=p'_u(1)[2]\operatorname{sp}_Y$ is equivalent to $p_y=p_x(1)[2]\operatorname{sp}_X$. These are exactly the two residue conditions of [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex]. Thus potentiality downstairs gives every condition upstairs; when $f$ is surjective, Step 6 supplies a lift for every downstairs condition, proving the converse.

source.place: XVII, Proposition 3.3.1 applied to the pinnings; Proposition 2.4.3.3

proof.text: In the strict localization at $\bar x$, let $i:C\hookrightarrow X_{(\bar x)}$ be the reduced closure specified in the statement. The closed-immersion clause of [lem-per-prime-power-supported-calculus] identifies its two costalks with those of $K$. Its residue-field maps at these points are identities, so Step 2's induced pinnings are the original ones: $\operatorname{Cl}_{\mathrm{id}}=1$ by [lem-per-absolute-gysin-purity]. Apply [lem-per-finite-residue-gysin-naturality] to the finite map $i$ and use the same rank-one cohomology argument of Step 7. The actual residue transition, and therefore its pinning square, is identical for $K$ and $i^!K$. This also follows directly from the definition, which already constructs the transition using this $i^!K$.

source.place: XVII, proof of Proposition 2.4.4.1, first paragraph

proof.text:
By [lem-per-prime-power-costalk-reduction], $C$ is integral excellent strictly henselian local of dimension one, and its normalization $
u:\widetilde C	o C$ is finite and a universal homeomorphism, hence surjective; $\widetilde C$ is an excellent strictly henselian trait. The same node gives the finite purely inseparable closed residue degree $d$, a unit in $\Lambda$. Give $i^!K$ the pinnings of Step 8 (for $\delta_X$ restricted to $C$, a dimension function by Step 1) and $
u^!i^!K$ those of Step 2. Since $
u$ is finite surjective, Step 6 lifts the given $ ar yightsquigarrow ar x$ of $C$ to an immediate $ ar vightsquigarrow ar u$ of $\widetilde C$ lying over it. For this one pair Step 7 shows that the residue condition of $
u^!i^!K$ at $ ar vightsquigarrow ar u$ is equivalent to that of $i^!K$ at $ ar yightsquigarrow ar x$, which by Step 8 is the square of $K$. So that single compatibility is tested on $
u^!i^!K$ with the induced exceptional pinnings; no claim is made that it is the only residue condition of $i^!K$. This uses $
u^!$, not an identification of its pinnings with unscaled ordinary inverse-image pinnings: the transition for $C$ has the factor $d^{-1}$ prescribed in [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex], and the finite-field Gysin comparison keeps that factor. Neither this argument nor Step 8 assumes potentiality in advance.

source.place: XVII, Proposition 2.4.3.3 and the first paragraph of the proof of Proposition 2.4.4.1

split_report.summary: Expanded the pointwise construction and Gysin composition, transported the defined residue squares through strict localizations, and proved finite detection by cancellation in the general finite residue-naturality square. Reused existing dimension, supported-calculus and normalization lemmas; added one statement-only cohomological naturality lemma. Clarified the Noetherian hypothesis on etale restrictions, as in ILO XVII 2.2.1. No Lean was written or compiled.
split_report.blueprint: Nearest ancestor lem-per-artin-gabber-affine-curve, Step 3 in its earlier DAG proof: dimension-normalized Verdier duality, via the regular finite-coefficient local model. The current main-20261015 node is a statement only; this inherited ancestry is retained. Steps 1–3 realize quasi-finite pinning and composition, Steps 4–5 strict localization, Steps 6–7 finite detection, Steps 8–9 the curve normalization test.

reviewed.note: mechanical checks by tools/merge_delivery.py; mathematics reviewed in full by NT-cc-N7-ec788edfa (reviewer sub-agent of L); spot-checked: I read the item, the new node lem-per-finite-residue-gysin-naturality, all 27 cited statements and the source, ILO XVII 2.2.1, 2.3.1–2.3.3, 2.4.1.1–2.4.4.1 (with the proof of 2.4.3.3 and Lemma 2.4.3.4) and 3.3.1 (pp.264–270). The live item is still unsplit, and the only statement change is the narrowing to Noetherian étale restrictions. It is correct: an infinite disjoint étale union is not Noetherian, and ILO 2.2.1 assumes Noetherian schemes. The delivery proves 2.4.3.3 by cancellation in the 3.3.1 square instead of following the source's trait argument. This is not circular: the proof of 3.3.1 reuses only the reduction of 2.4.3.3, and its base case δ_Λ=0 follows from 2.4.2.1(a) and 2.4.3.4. The DAG closure of both files is acyclic. The new node is ILO 3.3.1 for Z/ℓ^n with vertical arrows Cl⊗1, then T, then the supported identification. Its types check, and it holds in the small cases: id, closed immersion, and normalization of degree p^r, where Cl=d matches the d^{-1} in the definition. It duplicates no existing node (I compared general-costalk-transitions (F_ℓ), higher-residue-transitivity, exceptional-costalk-gysin, potential-extraordinary-pullback and finite-closed-support-exchange), and its form is clean. Steps 1–5, 7 and 8 are checked hypothesis by hypothesis: quasi-finite ⇒ finite residue extension ⇒ δ_Y=δ_X∘f; the pinning built from π^!, Cl and T; composition; excellence via 07QU, 06LJ and weak étaleness; ind-étale transport; and in Step 7 a rank-one scalar argument that gives the pairwise equivalence. I made two repairs. In Step 6, descending and lifting specializations needs X_(x̄) localized at a geometric point to be X_(ȳ); I cited lem-trf-ind-etale-strict-local-invariance (already in proof_deps). In Step 9, the text said 'potentiality of i^!K is precisely the single square', which overlooks the other generic geometric points; I rewrote it to use only the Step 6 lift and the pairwise equivalence of Step 7 plus Step 8. All six batch-5 flags are accepted because none is a step of the trace formula or Poincaré duality: def-per-potential-dualizing-complex is a definition, lem-per-finite-type-dimension-function is Stacks 02JW, lem-per-ind-etale-closed-support-base-change goes through the generic derivedPlus adjunction, and lem-per-prime-power-costalk-reduction, lem-trf-finite-base-strict-localization and lem-trf-ind-etale-strict-local-invariance are generic strict-localization geometry (05WR/0GIP/04GH). The 13 declared tool_uses are all generic and accepted. No SGA is used.
